note: Tags are produced by case-insensitive keyword rules applied to the stated field. In a caption, the questions presented or a bill's subject line and title, one match assigns the tag. In a bill's digest one match assigns the tag too, but the sentences about state-mandated local costs are not read, because they name elections officials in almost every election bill. For the Voting Rights Act (federal) rule only the digest's sentences that contain the word 'would', which say what the bill would do, are read, because a digest also names the federal act when it describes existing law. The rule does not count the name of another act that ends in the same words: a state's act named after the state (the California Voting Rights Act, the Voting Rights Act of New York), a 'State Voting Rights Act', the Youth Voting Rights Act and the Native American Voting Rights Act; the phrases are those of this pattern: \b(?:Alabama|Alaska|Arizona|Arkansas|California|Colorado|Connecticut|Delaware|Florida|Georgia|Hawaii|Idaho|Illinois|Indiana|Iowa|Kansas|Kentucky|Louisiana|Maine|Maryland|Massachusetts|Michigan|Minnesota|Mississippi|Missouri|Montana|Nebraska|Nevada|New\s+Hampshire|New\s+Jersey|New\s+Mexico|New\s+York|North\s+Carolina|North\s+Dakota|Ohio|Oklahoma|Oregon|Pennsylvania|Rhode\s+Island|South\s+Carolina|South\s+Dakota|Tennessee|Texas|Utah|Vermont|Virginia|Washington|West\s+Virginia|Wisconsin|Wyoming|State|Youth|Native\s+American)\s+Voting\s+Rights\s+Act\b|\bVoting\s+Rights\s+Act\s+of\s+(?:Alabama|Alaska|Arizona|Arkansas|California|Colorado|Connecticut|Delaware|Florida|Georgia|Hawaii|Idaho|Illinois|Indiana|Iowa|Kansas|Kentucky|Louisiana|Maine|Maryland|Massachusetts|Michigan|Minnesota|Mississippi|Missouri|Montana|Nebraska|Nevada|New\s+Hampshire|New\s+Jersey|New\s+Mexico|New\s+York|North\s+Carolina|North\s+Dakota|Ohio|Oklahoma|Oregon|Pennsylvania|Rhode\s+Island|South\s+Carolina|South\s+Dakota|Tennessee|Texas|Utah|Vermont|Virginia|Washington|West\s+Virginia|Wisconsin|Wyoming)\b . For the Initiatives, referenda and recalls rule a match does not count inside a campaign-finance phrase, where a committee or a payment supports or opposes a candidate or a ballot measure, inside the words with which a digest says that an act the bill amends was itself adopted by initiative, or inside the name 'Unlawful Voter Initiative', which is a project of the Department of Homeland Security and not a voter initiative; the phrases are those of this pattern: \bballot measure committees?\b|\bcommittees? for or against (a|an|any|the) (initiative or referendum|state or local ballot|ballot) measures?\b|\b(support(s|ed|ing)?|oppos(e|es|ed|ing)|support of|opposition to)\b[^.;:]{0,60}?\b(candidates?|offices?)\b[^.;:]{0,40}?\bballot measures?\b|\b(support(s|ed|ing)?|oppos(e|es|ed|ing)|support of|opposition to)\b[^.;:]{0,60}?\bballot measures?\b[^.;:]{0,60}?\b(candidates?|offices?)\b|\ban initiative measure (that authorizes the Legislature to amend|approved by the (electors|voters))\b|\bUnlawful\s+Voter\s+Initiative\b . For the Redistricting rule a match does not count inside words that name a seat by its district ('the office of Representative from the Fourteenth Congressional District of Florida'), which say nothing about how districts are drawn; the phrases are those of this pattern: \b(?:Representative|Delegate|Member|Resident Commissioner)s?(?: (?:of|in|to) (?:Congress|the House(?: of Representatives)?))? (?:from|for) the [\w-]+ congressional district\b . In text taken from a PDF (questions presented, filings and opinions), a word that the document breaks across two lines with a hyphen is joined again before the rules are applied; the hyphen is kept where the document also writes the word with one, or the first part is one of these words, which begin compounds: 'case', 'half', 'party', 'race', 'self', 'three', 'two', 'vote', 'voter', 'well'. Where a docket has no questions presented, the full text of its initiating filing or opinion is read instead, and a rule must be prominent there: at least 5 matches, and at least 15% as many as the rule that matches most often in that document. In such a text '^' in a pattern stands for the beginning of the document and not of each line, because a PDF breaks its lines anywhere: a line that happens to begin with 'Initiative' is not a subject line that begins with the word. A tag with rule id tag-curated-1 was added by a maintainer where the rules miss the central subject of a case; it is shown with the passage it rests on, which is checked against the cited document on every run. Tags indicate subject matter only. They are not legal conclusions and can be wrong or incomplete.

otherRules.appliesTo: Which court cases are included, and which places they are linked to
otherRules.description: A maintainer lists the docket and the places it concerns in pipeline/seeds/cases.json, each with a short description and a passage quoted from a named document of that docket (the Court's Questions Presented document, the filing that opened the docket, or an opinion or order). On every run that refreshes the docket the pipeline fetches the document and checks that the passage is in it, ignoring white space, hyphens and dashes, letter case and the style of quotation marks, and reading Unicode compatibility characters (such as ligatures and superscript digits) as their plain forms, and that the passage names the place. The check shows that the document says this. It does not check the maintainer's description, and a passage from a party's filing is that party's account. A link whose passage is not found is not published; it is listed in the review queue.

otherRules.appliesTo: Dockets shown as coming from the same case below
otherRules.description: Two dockets in the dataset are shown as related when the Court's docket pages give both the same lower court and a lower-court case number for the same case. A district court case number is compared without its letter case and leading zeros, and its year, case type and sequence number must agree. Some districts number cases separately in each division, so two different prefixes of the same kind (two division numbers, or two sets of office letters) are read as two cases. Where one number has a division number and the other office letters, or only one has a prefix, the judges' initials after the number must be given on both and agree (so 3:21-cv-00259-DCG-JES-JVB and EP-21-CV-00259-DCG-JES-JVB agree). Other numbers must agree exactly. The Court does not state the relation; it is derived by this rule.

otherRules.appliesTo: A Supreme Court docket shown with the court of appeals case it comes from
otherRules.description: A Supreme Court docket is paired with a court of appeals case in the dataset when the Court's docket page names that court of appeals as the lower court and gives a lower-court case number that is the case's docket number. The court's name must agree in full, and the numbers are compared by their two-digit year and their serial number without leading zeros. A number that would name two cases of the court is paired with neither. Neither record states the pairing; it is derived by this rule, and each of the two pages links the other. Most dockets from a court of appeals have no such link, because the case below is older than the documents read or was not picked by the selection rule.

otherRules.appliesTo: Links between a bill and another bill, a case or a place
otherRules.description: A maintainer lists the link in pipeline/seeds/relationships.json together with a passage quoted from the official text of the named bill version or from the named court document. On every run that has that text the pipeline checks that the passage is in it, ignoring white space, hyphens and dashes, letter case and the style of quotation marks, and reading Unicode compatibility characters (such as ligatures and superscript digits) as their plain forms; a passage that ties a bill or case to a place must also name the place. A link whose passage is not found, or does not name the place, is not published; it is listed in the review queue. The links are a hand-picked subset: the absence of a link does not mean two records are unrelated.

otherRules.appliesTo: Subject tags added by a maintainer
otherRules.description: Where the keyword rules miss the central subject of a case, a maintainer may add a tag in pipeline/seeds/cases.json with a passage quoted from a document of that docket. The passage is checked in the same way as a link's passage, and the tag is shown with it. A tag whose passage is not found is not published.

otherRules.appliesTo: Which California measures are included
otherRules.description: A measure is included when its latest official subject line matches the published keyword pattern, after the phrases of the published exclusion pattern have been removed from it. The words 'initiative' and 'recall' count only in an electoral sense, so a programme named an Initiative or a product recall is not included. Both patterns and the number of measures they were applied to are published in legislation/index.json and shown under Coverage and selection.

otherRules.appliesTo: Conditions quoted beside a California measure's effective date
otherRules.description: A sentence of the latest mirrored text is quoted as a condition when it says that the measure, or a named part of it, shall become operative or take effect only if, when, upon or after something happens. The pattern is \b(This|That) (act|bill|chapter|section|article|part|division|title|subdivision|paragraph|subparagraph)\b[^.;]{0,80}?\bshall (become (operative|effective)|take effect|be operative) only (if|when|upon|after)\b|\bSections? (?:[^.;]|\.(?=\d)){0,60}? of this (act|bill),? shall (become (operative|effective)|take effect) only (if|when|upon|after)\b . Whether a condition was met is not recorded. A condition worded differently is not found, so the absence of a quoted condition does not mean there is none.

otherRules.appliesTo: Repeal dates quoted beside a California measure's effective date
otherRules.description: A sentence of the latest mirrored text is quoted when it says that the measure, or a named part of it ('This section', 'This chapter'), shall remain in effect until, or only until, a date or an event and as of that date is repealed. The clause applies to the provision the sentence names, not necessarily to the whole measure, and only if the measure is enacted. Where the sentence gives a calendar date it is recorded; where it names an event, no date is recorded. A sentence repeated in several sections is quoted once. The pattern is (\b(This|That) (act|bill|chapter|section|article|part|division|title|subdivision|paragraph|subparagraph)\b|\bSections? (?:[^.;]|\.(?=\d)){0,60}? of this (act|bill)\b)[^.;]{0,80}?\bshall remain in effect (only )?until (?P<until>(?:(?!\. [A-Z(])[^;]){1,300}?),? and,? as of (that|such) date,? (is|are) repealed . A sunset worded differently (for example 'is repealed on' or 'becomes inoperative on') is not found, so the absence of a quoted clause does not mean there is none, and a later statute may have changed the date.

otherRules.appliesTo: Which measures of Congress are included
otherRules.description: Every measure of the Congress named in congress/index.json is read. A measure is included when one of its titles (display, official or short title) meets one of three tests, tried in this order: the title names election law (the first pattern); the title has a general election word (the second pattern) and the policy area the Congressional Research Service assigned is Government Operations and Politics, or none is assigned yet; the title has an election word (the third pattern) and the policy area is one of the three listed with it. A measure in the policy area International Affairs is not included, because its titles speak of elections in other countries. Before a title is read, the phrases of the exclusion pattern are removed from it: procedure of the two chambers (a rule for the consideration of a bill, the election of the Speaker) and voting outside public elections (proxy voting, votes of shareholders). Each measure's page names the test it met and the words that met it. The patterns, the policy areas and the number of measures read are published in congress/index.json and shown under Coverage and selection. A measure whose titles do not say that it concerns elections is missed.

otherRules.appliesTo: The stage shown for a measure of Congress
otherRules.description: The stage is the furthest step among the measure's recorded actions, read from the labels the action rules assign: became law; vetoed; sent to the President; for a resolution of one chamber, agreed to (or not agreed to) there; passed in each chamber; passed one chamber; failed in a chamber; reported by a committee; introduced. It says how far the measure got, not what is happening to it now, and it is not an official status. The official record's own latest action is shown beside it. The stage 'Passed House and Senate, not sent to the President' (for a concurrent resolution, 'Agreed to in House and Senate') means only that the record has a vote of passage in each chamber. The two votes can be on different texts, as when one chamber passes the other's bill with an amendment, so the stage does not say that Congress has passed the measure.
order: Not agreed to in the House
Not agreed to in the Senate
Passed House and Senate, not sent to the President
Agreed to in House and Senate

otherRules.appliesTo: Which court of appeals cases are included
otherRules.description: Every case of the thirteen courts of appeals that GovInfo lists with an opinion or order issued since 2025-01-01 is read. A case is included when the court's own record gives it the nature of suit 441 (Civil Rights: Voting), or when one of its documents meets one of three text tests: 'long' (at least 8 election words, at least 8 election phrases and at least 2 election words in every 1,000 words), 'dense' (at least 8 election words, at least 3 phrases and at least 5 election words in every 1,000 words) or 'party' (a party or the case title names an election authority, and the document has at least 3 election words). The text tests are not applied where the record gives the case a nature of suit of another field of law (contract, torts, labor, intellectual property, securities, freedom of information), and a document with many labor-law terms is not read as an election document, because union representation elections are not public elections. A clerk's cover letter (rule cover-letter-1) is not counted. Counts are taken after words broken across lines are joined. Each case's page shows the tests it met, the document they rest on and the phrases counted in it. The patterns, thresholds and nature of suit codes are published in circuits/index.json, with the number of cases and documents read for each court. The rule counts words: it can miss an election case, and it can include a case that only discusses elections.

otherRules.appliesTo: An issue tag of a court of appeals case that a maintainer removed
otherRules.description: The issue rules count words. In a long opinion a rule can reach its count although the case is about something else, for example where a court compares the standing of its plaintiffs with that in the gerrymandering decisions. A maintainer may then list the case and the tag in pipeline/seeds/tag_removals.json, with the reason and a passage of the opinion that shows what the case is about. On every run the pipeline looks for the passage in the documents of the case, ignoring white space, hyphens and dashes, letter case and the style of quotation marks, and reading Unicode compatibility characters (such as ligatures and superscript digits) as their plain forms. Only if it is found is the tag taken off, and the removal is then published with the case and shown on its page under Issue tags, with the rule that had assigned the tag and the words it had matched. If the passage is not found, the tag stays and the entry is listed in the review queue. A tag is never removed because of who the parties are or how the case was decided.

otherRules.appliesTo: Court of appeals cases the selection rule picks that a maintainer removed
otherRules.description: A maintainer may list a case in pipeline/seeds/circuit_exclusions.json when the opinion itself shows that no public election is at issue: an election of another kind (a student council, a union, a company board), a record that classifies the case as a voting case by mistake, election cases cited only as precedent, or a dispute in which an election office is only the employer. Each entry gives the reason and quotes a passage of the opinion. On every run the pipeline looks for the passage in the documents of the case, ignoring white space, hyphens and dashes, letter case and the style of quotation marks, and reading Unicode compatibility characters (such as ligatures and superscript digits) as their plain forms. Only if it is found is the case left out, and the entry is then published in circuits/index.json and shown under Coverage and selection. If the passage is not found, the case stays in the dataset and the entry is listed in the review queue. A case is never excluded because of who its parties are or how it was decided.

otherRules.appliesTo: Court of appeals documents that are a clerk's cover letter
otherRules.description: Some courts send GovInfo the clerk's letter that tells counsel an opinion was issued, in place of the opinion. A document is read as such a letter when the pattern \bDear [^:]{1,60}:\s*(?:The court (?:has |today )?issued an? (?:amended )?opinion in th(?:is|ese) cases?|Enclosed is a copy of (?:the|an) (?:amended )?(?:opinion|order and judgment)) matches in its first 4,000 characters. The selection rule does not count such a document, and the case page says that the file is the letter and not the opinion.

otherRules.appliesTo: The district court a court of appeals case came from
otherRules.description: The opinion's own line naming the court below is quoted when the pattern (?:On )?(?:Appeals?|Petitions? for (?:a )?Writ of Mandamus) (?:from|to) (?:a |an |the )?(?:(?:judgment|order|orders|decision|final judgment)s? of (?:a |an |the )?)?(United\s+States\s+District\s+Court\s+for\s+the\s+((?:(?:Northern|Southern|Eastern|Western|Middle|Central)\s+)?District\s+of\s+(?:the\s+)?)([A-Z][A-Za-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][A-Za-z]+){0,3})) matches in the first 20,000 characters of the opinion. The state is the one the district's name gives. It says where the case began, not what it concerns: a case from one state can concern another, or federal law alone. Many opinions name the court below in another form (an abbreviation, a caption set in columns), and then no origin is shown; the absence of one does not mean the case did not come from a district court.

otherRules.appliesTo: Whether a court of appeals decision is shown as published or unpublished
otherRules.description: Read from the court's own entry for the case's latest opinion, decision or judgment in GovInfo's record, and from no other entry: 'Unpublished' when the pattern \b(?:un|non-?)published\b|\bnot precedential\b|\bnon-?precedential\b|\bnot for publication\b matches, otherwise 'Published' when the pattern \bpublished\b|\bprecedential\b|\bfor publication\b matches, otherwise nothing is shown. The courts' rules on what an unpublished decision is worth as precedent differ and are not stated here.

otherRules.appliesTo: Court of appeals cases shown as decided together
otherRules.description: Two cases of the same court are shown as decided together when each has a document of the same day whose text, reduced to its letters, is identical and at least 2,000 letters long. That is how a court files one opinion that decides several appeals. The record does not state the relation; it is derived by this rule. Such an opinion appears once in timelines, with the numbers of all its cases.

otherRules.appliesTo: Which states and territories each judicial circuit is drawn with
otherRules.description: The pipeline keeps a table of the states and territories of each circuit. On every run of the boundary stage it reads 28 U.S.C. § 41 and 48 U.S.C. § 1821(a) in the edition of the United States Code that GovInfo publishes, and compares the table with the statute's entry for every circuit. The map and the list of courts are published only if they agree, and each court's page quotes the statute's entry. A name in the statute that is not a unit on the map, and a unit on the map that the statute places in no circuit, are listed in geo/circuits.json. The circuit outlines are the Census Bureau's state boundaries merged by DemocracyHQ, not an official map.

otherRules.appliesTo: Timeline entries for a changed text version
otherRules.description: A text version is listed as changed when the paragraph-level comparison with the previous official version adds or removes at least one paragraph. The counts come from a standard longest-common-subsequence comparison of the extracted paragraphs.

otherRules.appliesTo: What a measure of Congress is about, in a list and at the head of its page
otherRules.description: Quoted from the summary the Congressional Research Service wrote for the measure: the beginning of the first paragraph that is a sentence (a summary opens with the short title on a line of its own, which is passed over). Nothing is reworded. The quotation runs in whole sentences until it is at least 220 characters long and never beyond 560; a first sentence longer than that is cut at a word and shown with an ellipsis. The same lengths hold for every rule below. The quotation runs whole sentences until it has 220 characters; a first sentence longer than 560 characters is cut at a word and marked as cut.

otherRules.appliesTo: What a measure of Congress without a published summary is about
otherRules.description: Where the Congressional Research Service has not published a summary yet and the measure is listed under a short title, its official title is quoted. A measure that is listed under its official title has no further line. The quotation runs whole sentences until it has 220 characters; a first sentence longer than 560 characters is cut at a word and marked as cut.

otherRules.appliesTo: What a California bill is about
otherRules.description: Quoted from the Legislative Counsel's Digest, starting at its first sentence that says what the bill would do (the pattern ^(?:This|The) (?:bill|measure|resolution|constitutional amendment)\b.*\bwould\b at the start of a sentence). A digest first describes existing law; that part is passed over. A digest without such a sentence is quoted from its beginning. The quotation runs whole sentences until it has 220 characters; a first sentence longer than 560 characters is cut at a word and marked as cut.

otherRules.appliesTo: What a Supreme Court case is about
otherRules.description: Quoted from the Questions Presented document the Court publishes for the case. The question is looked for in this order: what follows the words 'the question presented is:' (the latest such passage, since an order of the Court can amend the question); the sentence 'the question presented is whether ...'; the first of several numbered questions, with their number; the first paragraph that begins with 'Whether' or ends with a question mark; otherwise the beginning of the text. Lines the Court adds below the question (the grant, the argument calendar) are left out. The quotation runs whole sentences until it has 220 characters; a first sentence longer than 560 characters is cut at a word and marked as cut.

otherRules.appliesTo: What a Supreme Court docket without a Questions Presented document is about
otherRules.description: The passage cited for the first of the docket's links to a place is shown (rule cases-seed-2): a maintainer chose it from a document of the docket, and the pipeline finds it in that document on every run that refreshes the docket. The line names the document. A passage from the filing that opened the docket is the account of the party that filed it, not a finding of the Court. A passage that begins or stops inside a sentence is shown with an ellipsis. The quotation runs whole sentences until it has 220 characters; a first sentence longer than 560 characters is cut at a word and marked as cut.

otherRules.appliesTo: What a Supreme Court docket with neither a Questions Presented document nor a cited passage is about
otherRules.description: The entry that opens the docket is quoted, for example an application for a stay. It names the kind of request, not its subject; the issue tags and the court below say more.

otherRules.appliesTo: What a court of appeals case is about
otherRules.description: Quoted from the opening of the opinion the selection rule rests on. The layout of the opinion's first pages is read (poppler's pdftohtml), so that running heads, page numbers, footnotes and footnote marks can be told from the text by their place and type size and left out. The opinion begins after the line that names its author ('SMITH, Circuit Judge.', 'PER CURIAM:') or, where there is none, after the line that names the panel. Of its first paragraphs, up to the first heading and four at most, the first whose quotation speaks of the case is taken: it holds one of a list of words such as 'appeals', 'challenges', 'sued', 'district court' or 'we hold'. Where none does, the first paragraph is taken. Formulas every order shares ('This appeal was considered on the record ...') are passed over. A word the page broke across two lines is joined again, with or without its hyphen as the rest of the opinion writes it. The passage is then checked against the plain text of the same file, read by another program (pdftotext): its letters must stand there in the same order, in at most four pieces, since the plain text runs footnotes and page heads into the body. A passage that fails a check (too short, not ending with a sentence, a remnant of a page head in it, not found in the plain text) is not published, and the case then has no quotation. The quotation runs whole sentences until it has 220 characters; a first sentence longer than 560 characters is cut at a word and marked as cut.
